title: A Look at Dungeons of Infinity - Part 2
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jh22fly0d-k

Three full games in, Daniel (@dungeondive) returns with an informed verdict on *Dungeons of Infinity*: a good game hamstrung by its documentation, and about ninety percent of the way to a great one.

What works is substantial. Thirty small dungeon tiles lay out by direction — in some scenarios drawn from separate north, south, east and west stacks — so the same scenario can produce a sprawling east-west corridor run one game and an open square the next. Each tile's number cross-references four charts feeding four risk decks: chests, bodies, debris, events. And the threat meter is a timer he actively praises, which he notes is rare for him. It counts down as you explore, and when it hits zero the game doesn't end — act two begins, and Dungeon Lord cards start coming out. Tension, not an artificial finish line.

The complaints are concrete. An errata list still growing on BGG. A scroll whose misprinted symbol helps the monsters. Bows never labelled two-handed. A quick-start guide that doesn't teach the game, backed by a "rulebook" that is really an alphabetical reference — a miserable way to learn. He also wants more enemy variety, better shop gear, and a chest deck that holds more than gold.

Designer Jack answers every question posted; Daniel's advice is to wait for a second edition.

----

Daniel says he's not against timers when they're used like this — to start act two rather than end the game. Which games use a clock well?
